title: A New Bill Would Kill the H-1B Green Card Pathway. Millions of Indians Are in the Queue.
excerpt: The American White-Collar Worker Jobs Act proposes ending dual intent, shortening visas to two years, and scrapping OPT — a triple blow to the diaspora’s most relied-upon immigration route.
body:
A Republican congressman from Texas has introduced legislation that would dismantle the pathway millions of Indian professionals have relied on to build permanent lives in the United States.

The bill, titled the **American White-Collar Worker Jobs Act of 2026**, was introduced by Representative Chip Roy on Thursday. If enacted, it would end the H-1B visa's longstanding "dual intent" provision — the legal framework that has allowed holders to pursue permanent residency while working on a temporary visa. For the roughly 300,000 Indians currently in the green card backlog, many of whom have waited over a decade, the bill would not just close a door. It would remove the hallway.

## What the Bill Proposes

The legislation targets every major pillar of the current H-1B system. It would shorten the maximum visa duration from six years to two, eliminate the ability to extend status while awaiting green card processing, and require applicants to demonstrate they maintain a residence abroad with no intent to abandon it.

It would also scrap the Optional Practical Training programme entirely — the post-graduation work pathway that allows roughly 200,000 international students, a disproportionate share of them Indian, to work in the United States for up to three years after completing their degrees.

In place of the current lottery, the bill proposes a wage-based selection system that would prioritise higher-paying positions. The idea, supporters argue, is to prevent employers from using the programme to undercut American wages.

"The H-1B visa has been abused, allowing employers to routinely sideline American STEM workers in favour of cheap foreign labour," Roy said in a statement. "It's time to end this lottery-based pipeline and replace it with a system that prioritises merit."

## The Political Landscape

Arizona Congressman Eli Crane, a co-sponsor, called the bill a defence of "future generations" against corporate displacement. It is backed by US Tech Workers, the Immigration Accountability Project, and the Federation for American Immigration Reform — three organisations that have long pushed for tighter controls on skilled worker programmes.

The bill arrives in a political environment already hostile to H-1B workers. The Trump administration imposed a $100,000 fee on new petitions last September, effectively pricing out mid-tier contractors and staffing firms — the very companies that sponsored the bulk of Indian workers. Denial rates have climbed again under the second Trump term. A weighted selection system favouring higher wages took effect in February.

Roy himself is retiring from Congress, having lost a primary bid for Texas attorney general. That detail matters: it makes the bill less a campaign tool and more a legacy play, which immigration attorneys say could give it longer shelf life in committee deliberations.

## Why This Matters for the Diaspora

Indians make up roughly three-quarters of all H-1B visa holders approved in recent years, according to Pew Research Centre. The programme is not just a work permit for them — it is the entry point to a multi-year, often multi-decade journey toward permanent residency. Ending dual intent would force every H-1B holder to choose between building a career in the United States and pursuing a green card, a choice the system has never before demanded.

The OPT elimination would hit Indian students hardest. Without it, graduates who fail to secure H-1B sponsorship — a majority, given the lottery odds — would lose their only legal avenue to remain in the country and work. Thousands of professionals working in AI, machine learning, and data science could face uncertainty if they lose access to this pathway after repeated lottery rejections.

Companies may either become more cautious about hiring international graduates or seek alternative immigration solutions, including cap-exempt H-1B programmes and O-1 visas for highly accomplished professionals.

## What Comes Next

The bill has been referred to committee. Immigration experts are sceptical it will pass in its current form — similar proposals have failed in previous sessions, and major technology companies, universities, and business groups are expected to oppose it. But the direction of travel is unmistakable. Each successive proposal chips away at provisions that were once considered untouchable, and the cumulative effect is reshaping what it means to pursue the American dream on an Indian passport.

For the hundreds of thousands of Indians whose lives are structured around the H-1B-to-green-card pipeline, the bill is a warning shot — not because it will become law tomorrow, but because the arguments behind it are gaining ground with every election cycle.
